title: Two verbs for 'to be': ser and estar

cards.title: A new way of seeing
cards.body: Each language both allows and obliges you to perceive and express the world in a certain way. Spanish has two verbs for 'to be' and makes you choose between them.

cards.title: ser = characteristics
cards.body: Ser (source of es and son) describes what something is like. Un ser = a being.

cards.title: estar = states
cards.body: Estar (related to 'state') describes a state you're in. Being tired and where you are are states; being a good or bad person is a characteristic.

cards.title: Not 'temporary vs permanent'
cards.body: Ask 'state or characteristic?', not 'temporary or permanent?'. That shortcut works most of the time but misleads: your job (even for five minutes) counts as a characteristic, so it takes ser. Some adjectives work with both verbs, with different meanings.

cards.title: estar: estoy, está, están, estás, estamos
cards.body: Estoy ends in -oy like voy. Estar is the only present-tense verb stressed on the ending: esTOY, esTÁ, esTÁN, esTÁS. Estamos is stressed as normal.

examples.en: I am / he is / they are / you are / we are

cards.title: cansado = tired (a state)
cards.body: The ending agrees with who is tired.

cards.title: Always tired — still estar
cards.body: Tiredness is a state however often it happens. Siempre can go almost anywhere.

examples.es: Siempre estoy cansado. / Estoy siempre cansado.

cards.title: Death is a state: estoy muerto
cards.body: Spanish treats 'dead' as a state, so it uses estar. 'Estoy muerto' is also slang for 'I'm exhausted'.

practice.why: ser as a noun: a being.
Dead is a state in Spanish.
